nameStory: The bottlebrush shield lichen gets its name from its distinctive branching structure that looks remarkably like a tiny bottle brush used for cleaning narrow containers. When you look closely at the edges of this lichen, you'll see numerous small, finger-like projections that create that unmistakable bottlebrush appearance. The 'shield' part comes from its broad, flat, shield-like overall shape that's characteristic of many lichens in this family.
description: Bottlebrush shield lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms broad, grayish patches on tree bark throughout New England. It has a distinctive flat, shield-like shape with deeply divided lobes that branch out like fingers. The lichen can grow quite large over many years, sometimes reaching several inches across, and has a somewhat leathery texture when dry. Its most recognizable feature is the abundance of tiny, branching projections along the edges that give it that bottlebrush look.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic bottlebrush-like projections along the edges - tiny, branching structures that feel slightly rough to the touch and create a frilly appearance around the perimeter

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms broad, flat, leafy patches that lie fairly close to the bark surface with deeply divided lobes radiating outward from the center

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green when moist, becoming pale gray or whitish when dry, with the underside typically darker

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on tree bark, particularly favoring hardwood trees like oaks and maples, rarely on rocks

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can grow quite large over time, often 2-4 inches across, sometimes larger on older trees

habitat: You'll find bottlebrush shield lichen growing on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, from lowland areas to moderate elevations. It particularly favors hardwood trees like oaks, maples, and birches, where it forms conspicuous patches on trunk bark and larger branches. Look for it in both mature forests and woodland edges where there's good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: Appears grayish-green and more vibrant during wet spring weather, making it easier to spot against darker bark. The bottlebrush edges are most pronounced when the lichen is hydrated from spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Often appears pale and dried out during hot, dry periods, but the distinctive edge structure remains clearly visible for identification purposes.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture brings back the grayish-green coloration, and the lichen becomes more noticeable as leaves fall and expose more bark surface.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round and actually becomes more conspicuous on snow-covered bark. Winter moisture keeps it relatively well-hydrated and identifiable.

funFact: This lichen was confused with its close relative for so long that scientists needed DNA analysis to finally prove they were separate species - thousands of museum specimens had been mislabeled for decades until molecular techniques revealed the truth!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with salted shield lichen (Parmelia saxatilis), but bottlebrush shield lichen has those distinctive branching, bottlebrush-like projections along the edges, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges. Memory trick: if it looks like it could clean a bottle, it's the bottlebrush!
contextualKnowledge: The genus Parmelia includes many similar-looking 'shield lichens' that were historically very difficult to tell apart without microscopic examination. Modern DNA analysis has revolutionized lichen identification and revealed that many specimens in museums and herbaria had been misidentified for generations.
compareHints: Bottlebrush shield lichen stands out from other Parmelia species by its distinctive branching edge projections - netted shield lichen has a more reticulated (net-like) surface pattern, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges. The bottlebrush projections are created by specialized structures called rhizines that are arranged differently than in its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Netted shield lichen is distinguished from its shield lichen relatives by its unique white net pattern - bottlebrush shield lichen has tiny finger-like projections, while salted shield lichen has a more uniformly smooth surface with white spots rather than a connected network.
Unlike its cousin the Netted Shield Lichen which has raised white ridges forming a net pattern, Salted Shield Lichen has scattered granular patches.

Unlike Netted Shield Lichen which has a distinctly white, net-like pattern on its surface, or Bottlebrush Shield Lichen with its fuzzy, hair-like projections, Smoky Crottle has a relatively smooth surface.
Among the shield lichens, fertile shield lichen is distinguished by its pale, prominent pores and frequent fruiting body production.
